probabilityNote: Probability is an estimate of how likely a question is, based on the weight of each topic in the INC syllabus and the usual style of B.Sc Nursing anatomy papers. It is not a promise.

questions.question: Define tissue. Classify epithelial tissue with the location of each type. Add a note on the nursing importance of epithelial membranes.
questions.answer:
1. Tissue: a group of similar cells with their intercellular material working together for one function. Four types: epithelial, connective, muscle, nervous.
2. Features of epithelium: closely packed cells, little matrix, rest on a basement membrane, no blood vessels, high power of regeneration.
3. Simple squamous: one layer of flat cells — alveoli, endothelium of vessels, serous membranes.
4. Simple cuboidal: kidney tubules, thyroid follicles, gland ducts.
5. Simple columnar (with goblet cells, microvilli): stomach and intestines.
6. Ciliated columnar: uterine tubes. Pseudostratified ciliated columnar: trachea and bronchi.
7. Stratified squamous keratinised: skin. Non-keratinised: mouth, oesophagus, vagina, cornea.
8. Transitional: urinary bladder, ureters (stretches).
9. Glandular epithelium forms exocrine and endocrine glands.
10. Diagram: rows of cells of each shape on a basement membrane.
11. Nursing: skin and mucous membranes are the first barrier against infection — oral care, skin care and perineal care keep them intact; ciliated lining is damaged by smoking.

questions.question: Explain the anatomical position, the anatomical planes and the terms used to describe movements. Give examples relevant to nursing.
questions.answer:
1. Anatomical position: upright, face forward, arms at the sides with palms forward, feet together; left and right are the patient's.
2. Directional terms: anterior/posterior, superior/inferior, medial/lateral, proximal/distal, superficial/deep, prone/supine, palmar/plantar — each with an example (the elbow is proximal to the wrist).
3. Planes: sagittal (right and left; mid-sagittal gives equal halves), coronal/frontal (front and back), transverse/axial/horizontal (upper and lower), oblique.
4. Movements: flexion and extension, abduction and adduction, medial and lateral rotation, supination and pronation, inversion and eversion, plantar flexion and dorsiflexion, circumduction.
5. Simple diagram of the three planes through a standing figure.
6. Nursing: accurate documentation of wound sites, positioning (supine, prone, lateral), range-of-motion exercises, reading CT/MRI sections, landmarks for injections and chest compression.

questions.question: Compare skeletal, smooth and cardiac muscle.
questions.answer:
1. Location: skeletal — attached to bones; smooth — walls of hollow organs and vessels; cardiac — heart.
2. Cell shape: long cylindrical / spindle / short branched.
3. Nuclei: many and peripheral / one central / one central.
4. Striations: present / absent / present.
5. Intercalated discs: only cardiac.
6. Control: voluntary / involuntary / involuntary with its own pacemaker.
7. Contraction: fast and fatiguing / slow and sustained / rhythmic and tireless.
(Present as a table.)

questions.question: Describe the types of cartilage with their locations.
questions.answer:
1. Cartilage: firm flexible connective tissue; chondrocytes in lacunae; no blood vessels, nourished from the perichondrium, so heals slowly.
2. Hyaline: glassy matrix with fine collagen — articular surfaces, costal cartilages, trachea, nose, larynx, growth plates, fetal skeleton.
3. Fibrocartilage: thick collagen bundles, strongest — intervertebral discs, symphysis pubis, knee menisci.
4. Elastic: many elastic fibres, springy — pinna, epiglottis, auditory tube.
5. Nursing: poor healing of joint cartilage; disc injury from wrong lifting.

questions.question: Describe the structure of a cell with a labelled diagram.
questions.answer:
1. Plasma membrane: phospholipid bilayer with proteins and cholesterol; controls entry and exit.
2. Cytoplasm with organelles: mitochondria (ATP), ribosomes (protein synthesis), rough and smooth ER, Golgi apparatus (packaging), lysosomes (digestion), centrosome (spindle), cytoskeleton.
3. Nucleus: nuclear envelope with pores, chromatin (46 chromosomes), nucleolus (ribosomal RNA).
4. Labelled diagram showing all parts.

questions.question: Classify membranes of the body. Describe serous membranes.
questions.answer:
1. Types: mucous, serous, synovial, cutaneous (skin), meninges.
2. Serous membrane: two layers of simple squamous epithelium on thin connective tissue — parietal (lines the cavity) and visceral (covers the organ) with a little serous fluid between.
3. Examples: pleura, pericardium, peritoneum.
4. Function: lets organs move without friction.
5. Excess fluid causes pleural effusion, pericardial effusion, ascites.

questions.question: Differentiate mitosis from meiosis.
questions.answer: Mitosis: one division of body cells giving 2 identical cells with 46 chromosomes, for growth and repair. Meiosis: two divisions in gonads giving 4 different cells with 23 chromosomes, for gametes.

questions.question: Classify glands according to the mode of secretion with an example of each.
questions.answer: Merocrine — secretion by exocytosis, cell intact (salivary glands); apocrine — tip of cell shed (axillary sweat glands, breast); holocrine — whole cell breaks down (sebaceous glands).

questions.question: What is the anatomical position?
questions.answer: Body upright, head and eyes facing forward, arms by the sides with palms facing forward, feet flat and together; all terms of position refer to it.

questions.question: Describe the structure of the lungs with a diagram. Compare the right and left lungs.
questions.answer:
1. Position: two cone-shaped spongy organs in the thoracic cavity on either side of the mediastinum, each in its pleural sac.
2. External features: apex (2.5 cm above the clavicle), base on the diaphragm, costal and mediastinal surfaces, borders; hilum with bronchus, pulmonary artery, pulmonary veins, bronchial vessels, nerves, lymphatics.
3. Right lung: 3 lobes, oblique and horizontal fissures, shorter and wider, 10 bronchopulmonary segments.
4. Left lung: 2 lobes, oblique fissure only, cardiac notch and lingula, longer and narrower.
5. Bronchial tree inside the lung: lobar → segmental bronchi → bronchioles → terminal → respiratory bronchioles → alveolar ducts → alveoli.
6. Alveoli: type I cells (gas exchange), type II cells (surfactant), macrophages; respiratory membrane under 1 µm.
7. Pleura: visceral and parietal layers with pleural cavity.
8. Blood supply: pulmonary vessels for gas exchange; bronchial arteries nourish lung tissue.
9. Labelled diagram of both lungs with lobes and fissures.
10. Nursing: positioning, postural drainage of segments, chest drain, auscultation of each lobe.

questions.question: Name the muscles of respiration. Describe the structure of the diaphragm and explain how the muscles bring about inspiration and expiration.
questions.answer:
1. Quiet inspiration: diaphragm (main) and external intercostals.
2. Forced inspiration (accessory): sternocleidomastoid, scalenes, pectoralis minor, serratus anterior.
3. Quiet expiration: passive recoil. Forced expiration: internal intercostals and abdominal muscles (rectus abdominis, obliques, transversus abdominis).
4. Diaphragm: dome-shaped skeletal muscle separating thorax and abdomen, peripheral muscle and central tendon; openings — vena caval T8, oesophageal T10, aortic T12; nerve — phrenic (C3–C5).
5. Inspiration: diaphragm contracts and flattens (vertical diameter ↑), external intercostals raise ribs (pump-handle and bucket-handle) → thoracic volume ↑, pressure ↓, air flows in.
6. Expiration: muscles relax, elastic recoil, volume ↓, pressure ↑, air flows out.
7. Diagram of diaphragm and rib movement.
8. Nursing: Fowler's position, deep breathing and incentive spirometry after surgery, high spinal injury affects the phrenic nerve.

questions.question: Describe the structure of the trachea.
questions.answer:
1. Tube 10–12 cm long, 2–2.5 cm wide, from C6 (lower border of cricoid) to sternal angle (T4–T5) where it divides at the carina.
2. 16–20 C-shaped hyaline cartilage rings open behind; gap closed by trachealis muscle, allowing oesophagus to expand.
3. Lining: pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium with goblet cells — mucociliary escalator.
4. Relations: oesophagus behind, thyroid isthmus in front of rings 2–4, great vessels.
5. Nursing: tracheostomy below the cricoid, carina touched during suction causes coughing.

questions.question: Describe the pleura and its nursing importance.
questions.answer:
1. Serous membrane around each lung.
2. Visceral pleura covers the lung and dips into fissures; parietal pleura lines chest wall, diaphragm, mediastinum.
3. Pleural cavity: potential space with a thin film of fluid; lubricates and holds the lung to the chest wall.
4. Parietal pleura is pain-sensitive; visceral is not.
5. Nursing: pneumothorax, pleural effusion, empyema, haemothorax; chest drain care; pleuritic pain on breathing.

questions.question: Describe the structure of the larynx.
questions.answer:
1. In the neck, C3–C6, between pharynx and trachea.
2. Cartilages: thyroid (Adam's apple), cricoid (complete ring), epiglottis (elastic, closes inlet), paired arytenoids, corniculate, cuneiform.
3. Vocal cords stretch from thyroid to arytenoids; glottis between them; vestibular folds above.
4. Cricothyroid membrane — emergency airway.
5. Nerve: recurrent laryngeal nerves (vagus) — injury causes hoarseness.

questions.question: Describe the bronchial tree. Why does an inhaled foreign body usually enter the right bronchus?
questions.answer:
1. Trachea → right and left main bronchi → lobar (3 right, 2 left) → segmental → bronchioles → terminal bronchioles → respiratory bronchioles → alveolar ducts → alveoli.
2. Cartilage decreases and smooth muscle increases as tubes become smaller; bronchioles have no cartilage.
3. Right main bronchus is shorter (2.5 cm), wider and more vertical, almost in line with the trachea, so foreign bodies and deep endotracheal tubes enter it.
4. Left bronchus is longer (5 cm), narrower, more horizontal under the aortic arch.

questions.question: What is surfactant? Which cells secrete it?
questions.answer: A lipoprotein that lowers surface tension in the alveoli and prevents their collapse; secreted by type II alveolar cells (pneumocytes).

questions.question: Name the paranasal sinuses.
questions.answer: Frontal, maxillary, sphenoidal and ethmoidal sinuses; they lighten the skull and add resonance to the voice.

questions.question: Name the openings in the diaphragm with their vertebral levels.
questions.answer: Vena caval opening at T8, oesophageal opening at T10, aortic opening at T12.

questions.question: Describe the structure of the stomach with a labelled diagram. Add its nursing implications.
questions.answer:
1. Position: J-shaped, epigastric, left hypochondriac and umbilical regions, below the diaphragm.
2. Parts: cardia, fundus, body, pyloric antrum, pyloric canal, pyloric sphincter; lesser and greater curvatures (lesser and greater omentum).
3. Relations: diaphragm, liver, spleen, pancreas behind (stomach bed), transverse colon below.
4. Wall: mucosa with rugae and gastric pits, submucosa, three muscle layers (outer longitudinal, middle circular, inner oblique), serosa.
5. Gastric glands: mucous cells, chief cells (pepsinogen), parietal cells (HCl, intrinsic factor), G cells (gastrin).
6. Blood supply: branches of the coeliac trunk; venous drainage to portal vein. Nerves: vagus and sympathetic.
7. Labelled diagram.
8. Nursing: nasogastric tube insertion and confirming position, gastric lavage, aspiration risk, peptic ulcer care, B12 deficiency after gastrectomy.

questions.question: Describe the structure of the liver and the biliary tract.
questions.answer:
1. Largest gland, about 1.5 kg, right hypochondrium and epigastrium under the diaphragm, protected by lower ribs.
2. Lobes: right, left (falciform ligament), caudate and quadrate.
3. Porta hepatis: hepatic artery and portal vein enter; hepatic ducts leave. Hepatic veins drain into IVC.
4. Capsule and peritoneal covering.
5. Lobule: hexagonal, central vein, plates of hepatocytes, sinusoids with Kupffer cells, portal triads at corners (hepatic artery branch, portal vein branch, bile ductule).
6. Biliary tract: right + left hepatic ducts → common hepatic duct; + cystic duct → common bile duct; joins pancreatic duct at the ampulla of Vater in the 2nd part of duodenum, guarded by sphincter of Oddi.
7. Gallbladder: fundus, body, neck; stores and concentrates bile.
8. Diagrams: liver lobule and biliary tree.
9. Nursing: liver biopsy positioning, jaundice from bile duct obstruction, care in cholecystectomy.

questions.question: Describe the structure of the small intestine. How is it adapted for absorption?
questions.answer:
1. 5–6 m from pylorus to ileocaecal valve: duodenum (25 cm, C-shaped, ampulla of Vater, Brunner's glands), jejunum, ileum (Peyer's patches).
2. Wall: four layers.
3. Adaptations: circular folds, villi with capillaries and lacteals, microvilli (brush border), crypts of Lieberkühn; long length.
4. Diagram of a villus.

questions.question: Describe the salivary glands.
questions.answer:
1. Parotid: largest, in front of and below the ear, Stensen's duct opens opposite the upper second molar, serous secretion; affected in mumps.
2. Submandibular: below the jaw, Wharton's duct opens beside the frenulum, mixed secretion.
3. Sublingual: smallest, under the tongue, many small ducts, mainly mucous.
4. Nerve supply: parasympathetic increases watery saliva.
5. Nursing: oral care prevents parotitis.

questions.question: Describe the structure of the pancreas.
questions.answer:
1. Soft lobulated gland 12–15 cm, retroperitoneal, behind the stomach.
2. Parts: head (in duodenal curve), neck, body, tail (near spleen).
3. Exocrine acini (most of the gland) drain into the main pancreatic duct, which joins the common bile duct at the ampulla of Vater.
4. Endocrine islets of Langerhans: alpha, beta, delta cells.
5. Blood supply from splenic and pancreaticoduodenal arteries.

questions.question: Describe the general structure of the wall of the alimentary canal.
questions.answer:
1. Mucosa: epithelium (stratified squamous in mouth, oesophagus, anal canal; columnar elsewhere), lamina propria, muscularis mucosae.
2. Submucosa: vessels, lymphatics, Meissner's plexus.
3. Muscularis externa: inner circular and outer longitudinal smooth muscle with Auerbach's plexus — peristalsis.
4. Serosa (visceral peritoneum) or adventitia.
5. Diagram of the four layers.

questions.question: Give the dental formula of permanent teeth.
questions.answer: In each quarter of the mouth: 2 incisors, 1 canine, 2 premolars, 3 molars = 8; total 32 permanent teeth.

questions.question: What are taeniae coli and haustra?
questions.answer: Taeniae coli are the three bands of longitudinal muscle of the colon; their pull puckers the wall into pouches called haustra.

questions.question: What is McBurney's point?
questions.answer: A point one-third of the way from the right anterior superior iliac spine to the umbilicus; it marks the usual base of the appendix and is tender in appendicitis.

questions.question: Describe the position, layers and chambers of the heart with a labelled diagram. Add a note on the valves.
questions.answer:
1. Position: middle mediastinum behind the sternum, two-thirds left of midline; apex at the left 5th intercostal space in the midclavicular line; base behind at T5–T8.
2. Relations: sternum in front, oesophagus and descending aorta behind, lungs at the sides, diaphragm below, great vessels above.
3. Size: about a closed fist, 250–350 g.
4. Layers: fibrous pericardium; serous pericardium (parietal and visceral = epicardium) with pericardial cavity; myocardium (thickest in left ventricle); endocardium.
5. Chambers: right atrium (SVC, IVC, coronary sinus; SA node), right ventricle (to pulmonary trunk), left atrium (4 pulmonary veins), left ventricle (to aorta, thickest); interatrial septum with fossa ovalis, interventricular septum.
6. Valves: tricuspid, mitral (bicuspid), pulmonary and aortic semilunar; chordae tendineae and papillary muscles.
7. Labelled diagram of the interior of the heart.
8. Nursing: apex beat, auscultation areas, chest compression, cardiac tamponade.

questions.question: Describe the blood supply and nerve supply of the heart, including the conducting system.
questions.answer:
1. Right and left coronary arteries from the ascending aorta above the aortic valve; fill in diastole.
2. RCA: marginal and posterior interventricular branches; supplies right atrium and ventricle, back of septum, usually SA and AV nodes.
3. LCA: left anterior descending and circumflex; supplies left atrium, most of left ventricle, front two-thirds of septum.
4. Venous drainage: cardiac veins → coronary sinus → right atrium.
5. Nerve supply via cardiac plexus: sympathetic (increases rate and force), parasympathetic vagus (slows).
6. Conducting system: SA node (pacemaker, right atrium near SVC) → AV node → bundle of His → right and left bundle branches → Purkinje fibres.
7. Diagram of coronary arteries and conducting system.
8. Nursing: chest pain, ECG, myocardial infarction care.

questions.question: Name the veins used for intravenous injection and describe the superficial veins of the upper limb.
questions.answer:
1. Dorsal venous network of the hand → cephalic vein (lateral, thumb side) and basilic vein (medial).
2. Median cubital vein joins them in front of the elbow — common venepuncture site.
3. Median antebrachial vein on the front of the forearm.
4. Other sites: great saphenous vein, dorsal venous arch of foot, external jugular, scalp veins in infants; central veins (internal jugular, subclavian, femoral).
5. Choose distal veins first; avoid joints, affected arm after node dissection or with fistula; brachial artery lies deep near the elbow.

questions.question: Differentiate arteries from veins.
questions.answer:
1. Direction: away from vs towards the heart.
2. Wall: thick muscular and elastic vs thin.
3. Lumen: narrow round vs wide, collapsible.
4. Valves: absent vs present in limb veins.
5. Pressure: high and pulsatile vs low.
6. Blood colour on cutting: bright red spurting vs dark steady flow.
7. All three coats in both: intima, media, adventitia.

questions.question: Describe the lymphatic system.
questions.answer:
1. Lymph capillaries (blind, permeable), vessels with valves, lymph nodes, ducts.
2. Thoracic duct from cisterna chyli drains most of the body into the left subclavian–internal jugular junction; right lymphatic duct drains the right upper quarter.
3. Lymph node: capsule, cortex with follicles, paracortex, medulla, afferent and efferent vessels.
4. Organs: spleen, thymus, tonsils, MALT (Peyer's patches).
5. Nursing: lymphoedema after node removal, palpating nodes.

questions.question: Describe the structure of the spleen.
questions.answer:
1. Largest lymphatic organ, left hypochondrium behind ribs 9–11.
2. Capsule with trabeculae; hilum for splenic artery and vein.
3. White pulp (lymphoid tissue around arterioles) and red pulp (sinusoids with blood).
4. Removes old red cells, stores platelets, immune role.
5. Nursing: rupture after left lower rib injury causes internal bleeding.

questions.question: Name the branches of the arch of the aorta.
questions.answer: Brachiocephalic trunk, left common carotid artery and left subclavian artery.

questions.question: Where is the apex beat felt?
questions.answer: In the left 5th intercostal space just medial to the midclavicular line (about 9 cm from the midline in adults).

questions.question: What are chordae tendineae?
questions.answer: Fibrous cords joining the cusps of the atrioventricular valves to papillary muscles; they stop the cusps turning back into the atria.

questions.question: Describe the structure of the eye with a labelled diagram. Add the nursing implications.
questions.answer:
1. Eyeball in the orbit, about 2.5 cm, cushioned by fat.
2. Outer fibrous coat: sclera and cornea (transparent, avascular).
3. Middle vascular coat (uvea): choroid, ciliary body (ciliary muscle, aqueous production), iris with pupil (sphincter and dilator pupillae).
4. Inner nervous coat: retina — rods, cones, macula and fovea, optic disc (blind spot).
5. Contents: lens with suspensory ligaments, aqueous humour (anterior and posterior chambers, drains via canal of Schlemm), vitreous body.
6. Accessory structures: eyelids, conjunctiva, lacrimal apparatus (gland → puncta → canaliculi → sac → nasolacrimal duct), six extrinsic muscles (III, IV, VI).
7. Labelled diagram of a section of the eyeball.
8. Nursing: instilling drops into the lower conjunctival sac, punctal pressure, eye care in unconscious patients, pupil checks, cataract and glaucoma.

questions.question: Describe the structure of the pituitary, thyroid and adrenal glands.
questions.answer:
1. Pituitary: pea-sized, in the sella turcica of the sphenoid, connected to the hypothalamus by the stalk; anterior lobe (glandular; GH, TSH, ACTH, FSH, LH, prolactin; via portal veins) and posterior lobe (nervous tissue; releases ADH and oxytocin); optic chiasma above.
2. Thyroid: two lateral lobes and isthmus over tracheal rings 2–4, C5–T1, about 25 g; follicles of cuboidal cells with colloid (T3, T4), parafollicular C cells (calcitonin); superior and inferior thyroid arteries; recurrent laryngeal nerve and parathyroids behind.
3. Adrenal: on the upper pole of each kidney within renal fascia; right triangular, left crescentic; cortex — zona glomerulosa (aldosterone), fasciculata (cortisol), reticularis (androgens); medulla — chromaffin cells (adrenaline, noradrenaline).
4. Diagrams of each.
5. Nursing: post-thyroidectomy voice and calcium checks, visual field loss in pituitary tumour.

questions.question: Describe the structure of the skin with a labelled diagram.
questions.answer:
1. Epidermis: stratified squamous keratinised, avascular; layers basale (melanocytes), spinosum, granulosum, lucidum (thick skin), corneum.
2. Dermis: papillary layer (papillae, Meissner's corpuscles) and reticular layer; vessels, nerves, hair follicles, sweat and sebaceous glands.
3. Subcutaneous tissue: fat, larger vessels.
4. Appendages: hair, nails, sebaceous, eccrine and apocrine sweat glands.
5. Diagram.
6. Nursing: pressure injury, intradermal and subcutaneous injections.

questions.question: Describe the structure of the ear.
questions.answer:
1. External ear: pinna (elastic cartilage), external acoustic meatus (2.5 cm, wax glands), tympanic membrane.
2. Middle ear: tympanic cavity in temporal bone; malleus, incus, stapes; auditory tube to nasopharynx; mastoid air cells.
3. Inner ear: bony labyrinth (perilymph) and membranous labyrinth (endolymph); cochlea with organ of Corti; vestibule and semicircular canals for balance; nerve VIII.
4. Diagram.
5. Nursing: pull pinna up and back in adults, down and back in children for drops.

questions.question: Describe the structure of the tongue and taste buds.
questions.answer:
1. Muscular organ covered with mucous membrane; anterior two-thirds and posterior one-third separated by sulcus terminalis.
2. Papillae: filiform, fungiform, circumvallate, foliate.
3. Taste buds: gustatory and supporting cells opening by a taste pore.
4. Nerves: taste VII (anterior 2/3) and IX (posterior 1/3); general sensation V; movement XII.

questions.question: Describe the structure of the islets of Langerhans and the parathyroid glands.
questions.answer:
1. Islets scattered among pancreatic acini, more in the tail; alpha (glucagon), beta (insulin, majority), delta (somatostatin), PP cells.
2. Parathyroids: usually four small glands on the back of the thyroid lobes; chief cells secrete parathormone.
3. Risk of removal in thyroid surgery → low calcium, tetany.

questions.question: Name the layers of the epidermis.
questions.answer: From deep to surface: stratum basale, spinosum, granulosum, lucidum (thick skin only) and corneum.

questions.question: What is the optic disc and why is it called the blind spot?
questions.answer: The point where the optic nerve leaves the retina; it has no rods or cones, so light falling on it is not seen.

questions.question: Name the ear ossicles.
questions.answer: Malleus (attached to the eardrum), incus and stapes (footplate in the oval window).

questions.question: Classify joints. Describe the structure of a synovial joint with a diagram and give examples of its types.
questions.answer:
1. Structural classes: fibrous (sutures, gomphosis, syndesmosis), cartilaginous (primary — epiphyseal plate; secondary — intervertebral disc, symphysis pubis), synovial.
2. Functional: synarthrosis, amphiarthrosis, diarthrosis.
3. Synovial joint structure: articular hyaline cartilage, joint cavity, synovial fluid, synovial membrane, fibrous capsule, ligaments; sometimes discs/menisci, bursae.
4. Types: ball and socket (shoulder, hip), hinge (elbow, knee, ankle), pivot (atlanto-axial, radio-ulnar), condyloid (wrist), saddle (thumb CMC), gliding (intercarpal).
5. Labelled diagram.
6. Nursing: ROM exercises, positioning to prevent contracture, joint dislocation risk at the shoulder.

questions.question: Describe the structure of a long bone. Explain the process of ossification and growth of bone.
questions.answer:
1. Parts: diaphysis (compact bone, medullary cavity with yellow marrow, endosteum), epiphyses (spongy bone, red marrow, articular cartilage), metaphysis, epiphyseal plate, periosteum, nutrient foramen and artery.
2. Microscopic: Haversian systems — central canal, lamellae, lacunae with osteocytes, canaliculi, Volkmann's canals; spongy bone trabeculae.
3. Cells: osteoblasts, osteocytes, osteoclasts.
4. Intramembranous ossification (skull vault) and endochondral ossification (most bones): cartilage model → primary centre in shaft → secondary centres in epiphyses → growth plate → epiphyseal line after puberty.
5. Growth in length at the plate; in width under the periosteum.
6. Factors: GH, thyroid and sex hormones, vitamin D, calcium, exercise.
7. Labelled diagram of a long bone.
8. Nursing: growth plate fractures in children, fontanelles, osteoporosis and fall prevention.

questions.question: Describe the sites of intramuscular injection with the muscles involved.
questions.answer:
1. Deltoid: 2–3 fingerbreadths below the acromion; avoid radial and axillary nerves.
2. Ventrogluteal: gluteus medius and minimus; palm on greater trochanter, index finger on ASIS, middle finger on iliac crest; inject in the V; few large nerves — preferred.
3. Dorsogluteal: gluteus maximus, upper outer quadrant; risk to sciatic nerve.
4. Vastus lateralis: middle third of the lateral thigh; site of choice in infants.
5. Rectus femoris: front of thigh, self-injection.

questions.question: Describe the vertebral column.
questions.answer:
1. 33 vertebrae: 7 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, sacrum (5 fused), coccyx (4 fused) — 26 bones in adults.
2. Typical vertebra: body, arch (pedicles, laminae), vertebral foramen, spinous, transverse and articular processes.
3. Special: atlas, axis with dens, C7 prominens, foramen transversarium in cervical vertebrae.
4. Intervertebral discs (fibrocartilage, nucleus pulposus).
5. Curvatures: cervical and lumbar (secondary), thoracic and sacral (primary).
6. Nursing: spinal cord ends at L1–L2; lumbar puncture at L3–L4 or L4–L5; safe lifting.

questions.question: Describe the structure of the knee joint.
questions.answer:
1. Largest joint; modified hinge between femoral condyles, tibial condyles and patella.
2. Capsule and synovial membrane with bursae.
3. Menisci: medial and lateral fibrocartilage.
4. Ligaments: patellar, medial and lateral collateral, anterior and posterior cruciate.
5. Movements: flexion and extension, slight rotation.

questions.question: Name the bones of the axial and appendicular skeleton.
questions.answer:
1. Axial (80): skull 22 (8 cranial, 14 facial), 6 ossicles, hyoid, 26 vertebral bones, sternum and 24 ribs.
2. Appendicular (126): clavicles, scapulae; humerus, radius, ulna, 8 carpals, 5 metacarpals, 14 phalanges each side; hip bones; femur, patella, tibia, fibula, 7 tarsals, 5 metatarsals, 14 phalanges each side.
3. Total 206.

questions.question: Name the rotator cuff muscles.
questions.answer: Supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor and subscapularis; they hold the head of the humerus in the shallow glenoid cavity.

questions.question: What is the epiphyseal plate?
questions.answer: A plate of hyaline cartilage between the shaft and epiphysis of a growing long bone where growth in length occurs; it ossifies after puberty to form the epiphyseal line.

questions.question: Why is the vastus lateralis preferred for IM injection in infants?
questions.answer: Gluteal muscles are poorly developed before walking and the sciatic nerve is close; the vastus lateralis is thick and away from major nerves and vessels.

questions.question: Describe the structure of the kidney with a diagram of the nephron.
questions.answer:
1. Position: retroperitoneal, T12–L3, right lower than left; 11 × 6 × 3 cm, about 150 g; adrenal on top.
2. Coverings: renal capsule, perirenal fat, renal fascia, pararenal fat.
3. Section: cortex, medulla with 8–18 pyramids, papillae, minor and major calyces, renal pelvis, renal columns, hilum.
4. Nephron (about a million per kidney): glomerulus + Bowman's capsule (renal corpuscle), PCT, loop of Henle, DCT, collecting duct; cortical and juxtamedullary nephrons; juxtaglomerular apparatus.
5. Blood supply: renal artery → segmental → interlobar → arcuate → interlobular → afferent arteriole → glomerulus → efferent arteriole → peritubular capillaries → renal vein.
6. Diagrams of the kidney section and nephron.
7. Nursing: renal angle tenderness, biopsy position, fluid balance chart.

questions.question: Describe the structure of the uterus and its supports. Add a note on the uterine tubes and ovaries.
questions.answer:
1. Hollow pear-shaped muscular organ in the pelvis between bladder and rectum, 7.5 × 5 × 2.5 cm; anteverted and anteflexed.
2. Parts: fundus, body, isthmus, cervix with internal and external os.
3. Wall: endometrium (functional and basal layers), myometrium, perimetrium.
4. Supports: pelvic floor (levator ani), transverse cervical (cardinal), uterosacral, round and broad ligaments; weakness causes prolapse.
5. Blood supply: uterine artery (internal iliac) crosses above the ureter; ovarian artery.
6. Uterine tubes: 10 cm; interstitial part, isthmus, ampulla (fertilisation), infundibulum with fimbriae; ciliated lining.
7. Ovaries: almond-shaped, cortex with follicles and corpus luteum, medulla; attached by mesovarium and ovarian ligament.
8. Diagram.
9. Nursing: fundal height, pelvic floor exercises, ectopic pregnancy in the ampulla.

questions.question: Describe the structure of the urinary bladder.
questions.answer:
1. Hollow muscular sac in the pelvis behind the symphysis pubis; rises into the abdomen when full.
2. Relations differ in male (rectum, prostate) and female (uterus, vagina).
3. Wall: transitional epithelium with rugae, detrusor muscle, outer coat.
4. Trigone between the two ureteric openings and the internal urethral orifice.
5. Internal sphincter (involuntary) and external sphincter (voluntary).
6. Nursing: palpable bladder in retention; catheter care.

questions.question: Differentiate the male and female urethra.
questions.answer:
1. Length: female about 4 cm; male 18–20 cm.
2. Course: female straight, opens in the vestibule; male S-shaped.
3. Parts: male — prostatic, membranous, spongy; female — single.
4. Function: female urine only; male urine and semen.
5. Nursing: short female urethra → more UTI; hold penis upward to straighten urethra during male catheterisation.

questions.question: Describe the structure of the breast.
questions.answer:
1. Over pectoralis major, ribs 2–6, sternal edge to mid-axillary line; axillary tail.
2. Nipple with lactiferous duct openings; areola with Montgomery's glands.
3. 15–20 lobes of lobules and alveoli; ducts → lactiferous duct and sinus.
4. Fat and Cooper's suspensory ligaments.
5. Lymph mostly to axillary nodes.
6. Nursing: breast self-examination, breastfeeding, skin dimpling in cancer.

questions.question: Describe the male reproductive organs.
questions.answer:
1. Scrotum keeps testes cooler.
2. Testis: tunica albuginea, lobules, seminiferous tubules with Sertoli cells, Leydig cells (testosterone).
3. Epididymis, vas deferens in the spermatic cord through the inguinal canal, seminal vesicles, ejaculatory ducts.
4. Prostate, bulbourethral glands.
5. Penis: two corpora cavernosa, corpus spongiosum with urethra, glans, prepuce.

questions.question: Define nephron.
questions.answer: The structural and functional unit of the kidney: a glomerulus with Bowman's capsule followed by proximal convoluted tubule, loop of Henle and distal convoluted tubule draining into a collecting duct.

questions.question: What is the trigone of the bladder?
questions.answer: A smooth triangular area on the inner base of the bladder between the two ureteric openings and the internal urethral opening; it does not stretch.

questions.question: Where does fertilisation usually occur?
questions.answer: In the ampulla, the widest part of the uterine (fallopian) tube.

questions.question: Describe the parts of the brain. Mention the functional areas of the cerebral cortex.
questions.answer:
1. Divisions: forebrain (cerebrum, diencephalon), midbrain, hindbrain (pons, medulla, cerebellum); brainstem = midbrain + pons + medulla.
2. Cerebrum: two hemispheres, corpus callosum, gyri and sulci, cortex (grey), white matter, basal nuclei; lobes — frontal, parietal, temporal, occipital, insula.
3. Functional areas: primary motor (precentral gyrus), premotor, Broca's speech area, prefrontal; somatosensory (postcentral gyrus); visual (occipital); auditory and Wernicke's (temporal); taste and smell areas.
4. Diencephalon: thalamus (relay), hypothalamus.
5. Midbrain (cerebral aqueduct, III and IV), pons (V–VIII), medulla (vital centres, IX–XII, decussation of pyramids).
6. Cerebellum: hemispheres, vermis, coordination and balance.
7. Meninges and ventricles.
8. Diagram of the lateral surface with lobes and areas.
9. Nursing: neurological observations, opposite-side weakness and speech loss in stroke.

questions.question: Describe the formation, circulation and drainage of cerebrospinal fluid. Add a note on the ventricles of the brain and on lumbar puncture.
questions.answer:
1. Ventricles: two lateral (in hemispheres), third (between thalami), fourth (between pons/medulla and cerebellum); lined with ependyma.
2. Formation: choroid plexuses, mainly in the lateral ventricles; about 500 ml per day, about 120–150 ml present at a time.
3. Circulation: lateral ventricles → interventricular foramina (Monro) → third ventricle → cerebral aqueduct → fourth ventricle → median (Magendie) and lateral (Luschka) apertures → subarachnoid space around the brain and cord.
4. Drainage: arachnoid villi into the superior sagittal and other dural sinuses → internal jugular veins.
5. Functions: cushion, buoyancy, waste removal, steady pressure.
6. Hydrocephalus when flow or absorption is blocked.
7. Flow diagram.
8. Lumbar puncture: L3–L4 or L4–L5, below cord end (L1–L2); lateral curled position; needle into subarachnoid space; observe for headache and leakage.

questions.question: Describe the structure of the spinal cord with a diagram of its cross-section.
questions.answer:
1. 45 cm from the foramen magnum to L1–L2 (conus medullaris); filum terminale; cervical and lumbar enlargements; cauda equina below.
2. Meninges and CSF around it.
3. Section: central H-shaped grey matter (dorsal horn sensory, ventral horn motor, lateral horn sympathetic T1–L2), central canal, white matter columns with tracts.
4. 31 pairs of spinal nerves from dorsal and ventral roots.
5. Diagram.

questions.question: List the cranial nerves with their main functions.
questions.answer: I olfactory — smell; II optic — vision; III oculomotor — eye movement, pupil, eyelid; IV trochlear — superior oblique; V trigeminal — face sensation, chewing; VI abducens — lateral rectus; VII facial — facial expression, taste anterior 2/3, glands; VIII vestibulocochlear — hearing, balance; IX glossopharyngeal — taste posterior 1/3, swallowing; X vagus — pharynx, larynx, heart, lungs, gut; XI accessory — sternocleidomastoid, trapezius; XII hypoglossal — tongue.

questions.question: Compare the sympathetic and parasympathetic nervous systems.
questions.answer:
1. Outflow: thoracolumbar (T1–L2) vs craniosacral (III, VII, IX, X, S2–S4).
2. Ganglia: sympathetic chain near cord vs near or in organs.
3. Fibres: short pre/long post vs long pre/short post.
4. Transmitter at organ: mainly noradrenaline vs acetylcholine.
5. Effects: fight or flight vs rest and digest (heart, pupil, airways, gut examples).

questions.question: Name the plexuses of spinal nerves with their important nerves.
questions.answer:
1. Cervical (C1–C4): phrenic nerve (C3–C5) to diaphragm.
2. Brachial (C5–T1): axillary, musculocutaneous, radial, median, ulnar.
3. Lumbar (L1–L4): femoral, obturator.
4. Sacral (L4–S4): sciatic (tibial and common peroneal), pudendal.
5. Nursing: protect radial, ulnar, sciatic and peroneal nerves when positioning and injecting.

questions.question: Name the meninges.
questions.answer: Dura mater (outer), arachnoid mater (middle) and pia mater (inner); CSF lies in the subarachnoid space.

questions.question: Where are Broca's and Wernicke's areas?
questions.answer: Broca's area (motor speech) is in the inferior frontal gyrus and Wernicke's area (understanding speech) in the back of the superior temporal gyrus, usually in the left hemisphere.

questions.question: What is the cauda equina?
questions.answer: The bundle of lower lumbar, sacral and coccygeal nerve roots in the vertebral canal below the end of the spinal cord (L1–L2).
